utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, distinguished gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue full well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And good morning to the members of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you and your team as I said. And appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, colleagues from the Prosecution. Appearing for Mr. Naser Oric are I, Vasvija Vidovic, and Mr. John Jones. Together with us today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you and your team. I take it there are no preliminaries. That's what I have been informed at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, no preliminaries. Just I was asked yesterday by the Registry to put on the record which exhibits we objected to. So I can just say that very shortly. It was Exhibit P468, P469, and P470. And we had already objected to P157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if I need to read the ERN numbers in that should be sufficient, I trust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Whoever is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can remain seated, Mrs. Stojanovic. We are proceeding and finishing with your testimony today. Now it's the turn of Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Mr. Oric. I just want to remind you of two things, namely that you are still testifying under oath, under the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday, in other words. And secondly that Mr. Jones is doing his duty here, and your obligation, your responsibility, in terms of your oath, is to answer all his questions truthfully and fully, unless we ourselves tell you not to. So, Mr. Jones, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Filipovic. I hope you're well rested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You called her Ms. Filipovic. Have I heard you well? She's not Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I was going to ask which she prefers. Sometimes it's Ms. Filipovic; sometimes it's Ms. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both are okay, but currently I am Mrs. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to start by asking you a little bit about what life was like in Srebrenica when you were there. You told us yesterday that you stayed in the Srebrenica area for approximately two months I think, staying with Hazim's two sisters at two locations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you weren't asked much yesterday about how you were treated during those two months. Weren't you in fact treated perfectly well?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't you become friends even with Mrki and his sisters?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you say that you retained even a certain affection for them even?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was with them I felt safe. I did not experience any particular fear. I spoke to them normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. It was very hard times for the people in Srebrenica at this period, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There was a severe food shortage, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. They did not have enough food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: People were having to make bread from bark and cornhusks because there wasn't enough proper flour?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were there a lot of shells falling on the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Srebrenica, but in the area where I was located, Solocusa, yes, there were shells falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were a lot of people getting wounded and dying from those shells?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not able to see. I was inside that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the hospital? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see people living out in the streets in the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the streets I did not. But I did see the families with which I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see people who didn't have a proper home to stay in and so they had to camp outside? That's really what I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see many refugees arriving in Srebrenica every day?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, apart from what you saw yourself, you must have spoken a lot to Hazim and his sisters and others when you were in Srebrenica. Did they describe life to you in Srebrenica as being as you just stated, namely very hard?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You agree that these were very difficult times in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's right that you and your children were kept in a house where it was warm, would you say, sufficiently warm?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I think from behind the glasses I am noticing that there is a problem. Usher, I can see that the distance between the microphones and the witness is too much. And also apart from the fact that the witness has to come near each time. I think we need to find a solution for that. Interpreters, thank you for bringing it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you always given adequate food at those houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always shared the same food that they had. We always took our meals together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you provided adequate clothing for you and your children, including for your baby?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't Mrki and his sisters make sure that you stayed somewhere where there was a cow so your children could have milk. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in summary then, would you agree that Mrki and his sisters treated you and your children in a way that perhaps you even had a better quality of life in many ways than many of the other people in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just dealing with Mrki for a moment - that's Hazim, Mrki, from Voljevica - is it right that you saw a lot of him during those two months that you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he often came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you had a lot of opportunities to see him from different angles and so you're very familiar with what he looks like?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that Mrki said, and I'm quoting, that "he physically resembled Naser Oric and many people confused them because they were so alike." Now, after the war did you see a programme on TV showing Naser Oric on a white horse and you thought it was Mrki?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. There were a lot of similarities in their physical appearance; they looked alike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's not answering the question. Let's divide it into two parts. You were asked whether after the war you saw a programme on TV showing Naser Oric on a white horse. Did you see such programme on TV or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't see him on horseback, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is no point putting the second question because she could not have mistook one for the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I ask a clarifying question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see Naser Oric on a TV programme at any time?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you saw him on that TV programme, is it right that you thought for a moment anyway that it might be Mrki?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, because when I was watching the programme the name "Naser Oric" was frequently mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us that you knew Naser Oric from before the war. Would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you agree that Mrki and Naser looked so alike that they could be described as being almost identical?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had known Naser from before the war; however, the image of him had faded in my mind. However, Hazim I met later. And when I would see cutouts from newspapers and photos, I found that you could mistake one for the other. They looked a lot alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell us what colour eyes Mrki had -- or has or had?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly how tall he was?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't very tall. He occasionally had a beard. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us that Mrki said that "many people confused them because they were so alike." Did Mrki tell you that happened often?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did tell me. He said that people often confused them, thinking that he was Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever see that for yourself if you were ever out and about with Mrki, people coming up to him and saying, Hey, Naser, something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you actually go out and about with Mrki much?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you get to know the personality of Mrki a little bit during your stay in Srebrenica? Let me put it this way: He had a lively sense of humour, Mrki, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was always cheerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you say that he was a bit of a joker, that he would tell fanciful stories, i.e., stories that weren't true?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the stories, but he seemed to have a cheerful disposition generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he would sometimes go to places and tell people that he was Naser Oric and they would give him food and other things, and he then would say, Oh, I'm not him actually.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that he sometimes used his resemblance to Naser Oric to play jokes on people?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was he a bit boastful sometimes, Mrki?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly. He was full of laughs and was, as I said, of a generally cheerful disposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not boastful. Boastful means -- sorry, Mr. Jones, if you want to explain it yourself, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, no, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there's obviously something different here. So go ahead yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was actually going to ask a slightly different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that you would sometimes take what Mrki told you with a pinch of salt and that you wouldn't necessarily believe everything he told you?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you sufficiently well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. Mrki told you that he sometimes acted as Naser's deputy. But would it be right that in the two months that you were in Srebrenica you never saw him and Naser Oric together? And so did you suspect that that might have been a boast which wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him with Naser Oric, and I never gave any thought to whether it was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Moving to a different subject. I'm going to go back to the day of your capture on the 14th of December, 1992. And firstly just ask you about some of the people who you saw when you were captured. And so we can probably go through quite quickly if you just say yes or no whether you recognised those people on the day. But firstly I just need to clarify, before the war you worked as a cook at the Sase mine. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that for slightly less than five years?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hired in 1985, worked until 1992. I stopped working at the mine on the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when you were captured you saw a number of Muslims whom you knew from the mine?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think you told us you recognised Mirza Hasanovic who you told us you were at primary school with?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was he brought in wounded into your house on the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And wasn't he on that day in fact kind to you and your children and tried to protect you from any problems you might have?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He tried to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Ramiz, whose house you stayed in in Poloznik, you knew him from the mine because he was a mine layer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you also recognise Mido [phoen] and his younger brother who were the sons of Edo, who was a porter at the mine?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Mido on that day. I didn't recognise among the people him or his brother, but I heard about Mido while I was detained and when I was in Poloznik village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And his father was Edo, who was a porter at the mine. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was a receptionist at the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a few more names. Did you recognise Senahid, known as Pobrin [phoen] who was a supervisor at the mine?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He also did a lot to protect us while we were detained in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you recognise someone called Hari?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name sounds familiar, but I can't recall anything at this moment. It eludes we at this moment, but I am familiar of the nickname Hari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be Hari Husmenovic [phoen] who was a football player for the Suba or Guba [phoen] team in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, Hari, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't most of the attackers you saw that day from Sase, Bjelovac, Voljevica, and Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were mostly attackers from the nearby village of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And weren't most of the attackers you saw in civilian clothes that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both civilian and uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But weren't they mostly in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. That was not what I noticed. There were persons wearing both civilian clothes and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for clarification. The question which has been asked of the witness, when you've asked whether they have been in civilian or other clothes, do you refer only to these people whom the witness knows or are there other people around --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. Thank you, Mr. Jones. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, no objection at all, just a matter that I suggest should be clarified. At the moment the questioning concerns the identity, the persons who were seen on the actual day of the attack prior to going to this other place of Poloznik. That's how I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems so, yeah. MR. DI FAZIO: We're all on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It seems to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now dealing with those villages, or those places, Sase, Bjelovac, Voljevica and Zaluzje, hadn't the Muslims been forced out of those places that had been living there at the beginning of the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's not something which you heard about later when you were in Srebrenica, that Muslims had been expelled from Voljevica, Bjelovac, your own village, Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. This is something I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you hear of a camp in Sase where a number of Muslims were kept?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know a Miroljub Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You wouldn't be able to help us with whether he was commander of a camp where many Muslim civilians, including more than a dozen children, were killed, camp in Sase?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Moving to another area. I want to ask you about a statement that was recorded as having been made by you on the 8th of October, 1994, and I should pass up copies of that so everyone has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the record, the English ERN is 03090984 to 03090989. And the B/C/S is 00652346, 00652352.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Filipovic, if you could look at that statement, do you recognise your signature at the bottom of each page?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention first to the section where you mentioned the Muslims you recognised after your capture. It's -- in English it's page 3, second paragraph, halfway down to the end of the paragraph. In your version, Ms. Filipovic, it's page 3, bottom of page 3, three lines, where it starts [B/C/S spoken]. We see there, and I won't read out the whole passage, but a number of names of Muslims, Mirza Hasanovic, Senahid, Miri?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that those details are all correctly recorded of the persons you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So whoever took that statement correctly recorded what you said about the people you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for this part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number to be given to this statement. I'm going to, obviously, come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I lost the sequence from yesterday, so I wouldn't know the number. It's D?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered by the accused and is being received and marked as document D164. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you can put that statement to one side. Do you recall making another statement just a few days after your release in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a lot of statements, quite a number of statements. I don't even remember to whom, but I gave quite a number of statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These are ones that we have and we'll show it to you. We're going to pass up copies. Again, the English ERN is 00366749 to 00366751.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The B/C/S version, just to explain a little, is from the rules of the road file. And so in the B/C/S version we have the first pages to show that it's part of the rules of the road file against Naser Oric. And that's RR321758. And then Ms. Filipovic's statement is RR321977 to RR321978. And as I think Your Honours noted yesterday, perhaps the Prosecution noted, that the English version is incorrectly dated 18th February, 1992, but it's an obvious mistake because it concerns the attack on Bjelovac. And the B/C/S version says 1993. And we also, just as a separate exhibit, we have a document which shows that this statement was submitted to the commission of experts on 18 May 1993, and that's being submitted, just to date the document. And the introductory pages are 017954 to 017958. And then her statement is at 018070 to 018072. And for the English I'll use the ERN version because that's easier for us all to track.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Filipovic, if you could look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give them a number straight away, Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- so that, if necessary, I may have to state something for the record as we go along, I don't know, but it may well be. So if we have the number straight away. The first one, the one which has ERN number 00136649 -- 648 to 650, this would be given Defence Exhibit 165. The next one which contains eight pages, the fourth -- the first five of which are -- have ERN number 017954 until 958. And the last three of which bear ERN number 018070 until 018072 is being given -- marked as Defence Exhibit D166. And finally, the exhibit -- the document which consists of three pages starting with the ERN number RR321758 and then RR321977, and finally RR321978 is being marked -- received and marked as Defence Exhibit D167.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Just two matters, I presume that for D164, the English and Bosnian, were both tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's always like that. And then one will be marked with an E. That's something that the registrar takes care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And secondly, I'm just not sure if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need to bother about that, because most of the time I have it in two languages, and the English version is always marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The other thing was just, I'm not sure if the six-digit number is technically an ERN. But anyway, it's not part of the eight-digit system, but it's marked with that number anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, Ms. Filipovic, if you could look at the statement that's been put in front of you. If I could ask you to turn to the last page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record, the witness is being asked to look at Defence Exhibit D167.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could put it on the ELMO, but it's in B/C/S. We don't have the English version of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the English version is these other two documents. It's identical -- D165 and D166 are identical in content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't have guessed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They correspond to this document, D167.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Filipovic, looking at the last page, do you recognise your signature there?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That statement ends with the words "they released me six to seven days ago." Could it be that you were released round about the 11th or 12th February, early February, in any event, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly occurred in February, but I can't remember the specific date. It was February for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to just briefly start again by directing your attention to where you mention the people who you recognised on the day of your capture. In the English version it's page 2, ERN 00366750, halfway down the page. In your version it's the first page, seven lines from the bottom, [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that? And in English it says: "Most of the attackers on Bjelovac came from the villages of Voljevica, Zaluzje, Biljaca. I know most of them by sight, not by name. Also in the group was Mido and his younger brother. Their father's name is Edo. Edo was a porter in the Sase mine." Now, that bit, it seems, from what you said today, is not entirely accurate, but it's right, isn't it, that you knew Edo from the mine?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a statement given by you on or around 18th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave quite many statements after I had left Srebrenica, quite many. I may not remember this specific one, but this may as well be one of these statements that I gave at the time. However, I wish to clarify something, Your Honours, if I may. All the statements that I gave several days after leaving Srebrenica and then up to two years later, there may be certain discrepancies between the statements that I gave four or five years later and the earlier ones simply because at the time -- I can tell that this statement doesn't quite tally with the statements that I gave several years later. I was still in a state of shock in the early days after leaving, and I was not even fully conscious what had happened to me over there. And then years passed and I became more and more aware of what had gone on and I started to remember more clearly. If any changes need be made to these statements or if there are discrepancies, this is something that I can always be asked to clarify, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm coming to. So let's move to matters of substance. Yesterday you told us how you were wounded on the 14th of December, 1992 by a grenade thrown by Muslim attackers. And I think - and correct me if I'm wrong - that you even sought to suggest that they knew when they threw the grenade that they were throwing it at women and children. And I say that because you said, and I'm quoting, it's page 14, lines 4 to 20: "When we climbed upstairs, the five of us, we hid in part of the loft that had been built out of wooden panels. However, they already knew that there was somebody inside and they searched the house. When they came in they saw children's schoolbags." Now, pausing there, you weren't actually there when the people came in, were you, so you don't know whether in fact they saw children's schoolbags or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were no children's schoolbags. Those were bags containing the clothing of my daughter and son.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. But you don't know, do you, whether the people who came into your house saw any of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't you speculating about what the people saw when they entered your house? You don't in fact know what they saw.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you don't know, do you, whether anyone seeing those bags would know whether the children were in the house or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But they knew that there was someone in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But that someone could be anyone, couldn't it? It could be a man, it could be a sniper, it could be a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Continuing with what you said yesterday. You said: "Before they came up they called out. They said, If there is anyone here, come out and surrender. They searched for a long time without finding us. They warned that they would throw a grenade from a hand-held rocket launcher called Zolja. They warned many times but we didn't surrender. We didn't come out of the hiding place. Then we left the house and we didn't hear anything else for a while until a very strong explosion from a grenade that fell into the loft through the roof. Both Brano and I were injured. Brano was sitting behind my back and my mother-in-law was leaning on the wall behind my back." And then you go on to say how you were wounded. So that is, isn't it, a very grim story in which, let's face it, the attackers come across as pretty inhumane, throwing grenades at women and children. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to the question. I heard the evidence yesterday, and I'm -- unfortunately I don't have all of the transcript in front of me. But searching my memory, I can't remember any innuendo or suggestions on the part of this witness that there was a deliberate act against women and children in the house. As I recall her evidence, and I also rely on the quote put by Mr. Jones preceding these questions, the witness was saying that she concluded that the attackers knew there were -- there was someone inside the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was someone inside the house. MR. DI FAZIO: So this notion of a cruel and inhumane attack or accusation -- the suggestion that this witness is trying to -- was yesterday saying that there was a savage or cold-blooded attack against women and children is, in my submission, not in fact what transpired yesterday. And on that basis, I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I perhaps should have continued with the quotation because later it goes on: "They were furious and they were cursing and swearing and suddenly one of them said, Oh, that's where they are." So I would put it to the witness that she was suggesting that they knew that "they," women and children, were in the house. In any event, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can skip this and move on to something else. I never -- at least I speak for myself. But during her testimony yesterday, I never felt that she was suggesting that in her mind she knew that they knew that there were only women and children up there and that they were going to -- I didn't get it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. There are more substantial details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's now go back to your 1994 statement and see what you said about these events when you were asked about them. And it's -- if you can take that statement, the 1994 one which is -- apologies, D164. And in English it's page 3, ERN 03090986, the first paragraph. And if you look, Ms. Filipovic, page 3, third paragraph, second sentence, it starts off [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 3 is in the B/C/S, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Page 3 of English and page 3 of B/C/S. It's first paragraph and it's second -- third sentence. I'll read it: "After a while a large number of Muslims broke into the house." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Do you have it, Ms. Filipovic? [B/C/S spoken], do you see that? Page 3, third paragraph, second sentence. "After a while a large number of Muslims broke into the house. And having seen that there was no one on the ground floor, they took up positions at the windows" --

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that on the page in front of me, and this is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... It's the 1994 statement, D164. And it should be page 3, third paragraph. And you have to go down to the third sentence [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can show on my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see that now, [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I'll read in English. "After a while a large number of Muslims broke into the house. And having seen that there was no one on the ground floor, they took up positions at the windows and starting shooting from there at the village defenders. After a while, three of them climbed up to the first floor in the attic to see if there was anyone there. I should state that before they entered the house I had found two grenades on the first floor that my husband had left and I decided to throw them at the Muslims in the yard. I detonated one of the grenades clumsily and tried to through it over the balcony. It bounced off the parapet and exploded, wounding Branko and me. I later threw the second grenade into the yard, but it did not detonate. However, some of the Muslims in front of the house were wounded by the first grenade." And then it goes on to say in the next paragraph that the Muslims, as soon as they found you, tended to you and Brano. I quote: "The three Muslims who were searching the first floor and attic found us and took us to the first floor. They immediately bound Branko's wounds and mine." Now my question is: You sought to explain that your memory has returned over time, your true memory, but isn't this a very specific, detailed account of throwing a grenade, it getting -- it bouncing off the parapet, exploding, a very specific recollection, which I put it to you is the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is not a faithful recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is this what you told the person who interviewed you firstly?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you see here is what I said to the person who was interviewing me, but a number of these data are simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you: How is it possible that you would remember the true event, as you say, that Muslims threw a grenade and injured you, which would in fact fit in better, I suggest, with the events of that day, of being attacked, how would that true -- how would that true memory get confused in your mind with a recollection of where you're throwing grenades and injuring people? How on earth could that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to clarify, Your Honours. We were hidden in the attic by that time. And as soon as they found out there was someone in the house they called for us to surrender, cursing and infuriated by the fact that they hadn't been able to locate us. They started yelling to the effect that they would set fire to the house, that they would kill us, that they would fire a Zolja. Then they left the house, and there was silence for a while. Later on they launched some sort of a grenade which caused a powerful explosion. Roof tiles began falling off overhead and we were wounded. As for the grenades, I did throw two. Several days later I saw grenades on a shelf in my father-in-law's house. I remember those grenades. I did throw two to try to protect my family and myself. I just tried to throw them out of the window. I didn't exactly know how to use hand grenades. I didn't realise that I was supposed to pull the safety pin out. I just threw the whole thing out of the window without removing the safety pin. There was yelling and moaning outside in the yard - that was later on - when we had already been captured and taken down to the ground floor. After a while a young man came in whom I knew a little. His name was Mijac and he was from Srebrenica. He had been wounded in the foot. He came into the house, and he asked me who was in the barn that was in our yard. The distance from the house was perhaps about 15 metres. I said it was my husband, because I was convinced at the time that he was still in the barn lying wounded. He asked me who was there, and I said, My husband. And he told me, Look what he did to me but then I had to kill him. However, after I while, when I was back from Srebrenica, I talked to my husband about this. And of course that person had not been my husband. That was a neighbour, Radovan Vucetic. He was in fact in the barn, and he shot and wounded this person Mijac, whereas I thought that it had been my husband who had wounded him. So it was only at this point later on that I found out what had really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it in light, if I understand correctly, in light of things which your husband said to you that you've decided that it wasn't your grenade which harmed you but it was the Muslims' grenade?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's not my husband who told me that it was not our hand grenade that hurt us. I know that for myself, because I know that they threw them out of the window as they were without pulling out anything. There was a lot of shooting at the time, and at the moment when I was throwing them out I may have thought for a second that they had exploded but they didn't. Brano and I were still together downstairs, and it was only later when we climbed up to the loft, to the attic loft, that we were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Filipovic, I'm not going to dwell on this subject overlong, but I suggest that what you've just given us is a very well-rehearsed explanation of why you've changed your account and that you came to change your account because people, Serbs in Bjelovac, told you it would be better to blame the Muslims than to say the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. She can agree that that's what's happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What you just suggested is something that never -- no one ever told me. It must be some conclusion of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I alone am in a position to know what exactly transpired there and I alone am giving you an account of what exactly happened. You can make your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. You alone know what happened. And before you went back to Bjelovac and spoke to your --

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. You alone know what happened. And before you spoke to other people and returned to Bjelovac, you were telling people that threw the grenade, it bounced off the parapet and exploded, "wounding Branko and me." That is your recollection which has been influenced by discussions with others. But you've replied to that, so I'll put another question and then come to your 1993 statement. These grenades, your husband got them from the Bjelovac TO or from the VRS, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never have I mentioned three hand grenades. There were only two hand grenades in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I said two -- I said "these," and that probably became three. Two grenades. Where did your husband get them from?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know even that they belonged to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Surely someone else didn't leave grenades lying around in your house. Did anyone else have access to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My father-in-law and my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So do you think one of -- it might have been their grenades that you found?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it's quite probably that either your husband or your father-in-law or your brother-in-law had grenades at this time. That's not something that would have surprised you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Jones, because at this point I have to intervene. The way she answered your previous question, I take it that she is being categoric, that these grenades belonged not to her husband but to her either father-in-law or her brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should ask her how she knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's confirm this first. Am I reading you well or not, Madam Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hand grenades could have belonged either to my father-in-law or to my brother-in-law or to Slavoljub. I didn't know to whom they belonged exactly. All I know for sure is that they were in the room usually occupied by my father-in-law lying on a self.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point is this: Yesterday I think you said that your father-in-law and brother-in-law and perhaps your husband, too, were civilians. My question is: Would it surprise you to find that they had grenades in their possession, as civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally they were civilians of Bjelovac. But they had rifles. Once these were issued to them, probably by the TO of Bratunac, so that they could guard the village, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So they were civilians who'd had rifles issued to them and who possessed grenades. Would that be a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true as far as the rifles are concerned. I don't know about the hand grenades, where they got them from. All I know is that they were in my father-in-law's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yet you say, don't you, that a Muslim in civilian clothes with a rifle is a soldier, but you seem to be saying that a Serb in civilian clothes with a rifle and even grenades is a civilian. Do you maintain that distinction?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to turn -- well, I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I should think you should.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's more for observation really than a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I could refer the witness to D165, which is the statement from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree, Ms. Filipovic, that this was the first statement which you gave, given that your signature appears next to the date of 18th February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. D167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D167 is the one you need to refer the witness to, because, as has been pointed out, D165 is the English translation of it. Thank you, registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first, Ms. Filipovic, you agree that this is the first statement you gave about these events, given that your signature appears Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. next to 18 February 1993 when you say you were released six or seven days before, or do you recall giving a statement even before that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember. I gave a lot of statements. I don't remember whether this statement is the first. All I know is that I gave a lot of statements after released from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Well, isn't it right that in this statement, which would be more than a year before your 1994 statement, you told the exact same story, not only that you threw a grenade, that it detonated on the balcony. If you like I will refer you to page 1, and it's RR321977. In the English, it's page 1, and the ERN is 00366749. Do you see the words, Ms. Filipovic, starting [B/C/S spoken] down to where it says [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that? It starts about a third of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it helps, I can give the usher my highlighted copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the meantime I'll just read what it says in English: "Seeing the Muslims entering our yard and shooting, we locked ourselves up in the attic. I heard them squabbling outside the locked door, you go in, I daren't, you go, there's no one there. I diffused a bomb and threw it out the window to save my family, my young children and my mother-in-law, but the bomb got caught in a balcony fence and injured me slightly. I later heard that the bomb had also injured a Muslim called Midhat Totanovic [phoen], but at the time they were not aware that it was my bomb that had hit him." My question is: Isn't that not only the same account, but it's the same in this very exact detail of the bomb actually getting caught in the parapet, as you described in 1994, the balcony fence, and detonating, and this appears to be a very specific memory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that in the original it says the bomb or the grenade grazed the fence and also in the last line, Midhat Totanovic, nicknamed Mijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question remains -- I'll put it slightly differently. Are you saying that not only the memory of you throwing a bomb which detonated is wrong, but the detail of it getting caught in the balcony, the fence, or the parapet that that is something which you never saw? I can simplify it even more. Did you never see the grenade which you threw get caught somehow after you threw it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this detail is wrong, both in your 1993 statement and in your 1994 statement? In your 1994 statement there's a reference to: "I detonated one of the grenades clumsily and tried to throw it over the balcony. It bounced off the parapet and exploded, wounding Branko and me." And in this statement: "I diffused a bomb and threw it out the window to save my family, but the bomb got caught in the balcony fence and injured me slightly." Don't you agree that that's a very similar description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment ago I said that it took me a really long time to realise the entirety of what had transpired and how it transpired. These two statements that you just quoted were given by me within a very short interval after I was released in Srebrenica before I actually knew what exactly happened there. Later, as time went on, as years went by - and maybe there are details that I still haven't recollected yet - I remembered things in pieces, like a jigsaw puzzle. It takes a long time to remember what exactly happened in every detail. And I repeat, there may be a lot of things that still elude me because the memory is very painful, one that I'm trying to suppress, however it is stronger than me and it keeps coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just two more questions on this subject. This isn't a case, though, is it, of having a vague recollection early on and then remembering a lot more detail later. I put it to you that these statements are actually very detailed right down to the people you saw, what job they did at the mine, what they said to you, and that this is very specific detail about what -- precisely where the grenade went, et cetera. So this isn't a case of memory coming back but of changing your memory. Do you accept that? In other words, it's not more detail; it's changed detail.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I do not accept that and I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally -- one more question on this point and it's really to be clear that of course there's nothing wrong or to be ashamed in throwing a grenade to protect your family. I want you to understand that it's not a reproach to suggest that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be a stupidity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is that it's wrong to come before this Court and to say that people injured you when they didn't do so. And I'll the matter at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to something different, Mr. Jones. Yes, Mr. Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Very short question. With regard to Exhibit D167, the statement we were talking about, where does it come from? There's no indication at all who had been the interrogator.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can just see my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Who was interrogating?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I can say about this statement is partly what I've already said, that it's submitted by the Serb authorities as part of the case against Naser Oric. The witness has accepted it's her signature. As to who conducted the interview, that may be something we can find out. We may not have that information present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the face of the document there is nothing. Unless the witness is in a position to enlighten us on this, we would never know unless you find otherwise the information.. Do you remember this first statement that you've seen, D167, this one, who was interviewing you, who you gave it to? Do you remember? Was it a police? Was it a judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't remember, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One final question on this, not on the statement, but when the Muslims found you in the attic, didn't Mirza Hasanovic say something like, Mira, why didn't you say it was you?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In other words, wasn't he shocked to find you there and regretted, in effect, finding you in such a dangerous place?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember, he asked me how come I was still there with the children, why hadn't I gone somewhere. I replied that I had arrived three or four days prior and that I was intending to leave that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So he wasn't expecting to find any women and children in Bjelovac -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to that question. This witness can't testify as to what the expectations were in the mind of this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you didn't live in Bjelovac from April to December 1992, did you, you just paid occasional visits to the village.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't living there. I just came two or three times in April to pick up some things for my daughter Olivera because I gave birth to my second child in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that you left because it was dangerous to remain in the village, because it had become part of a war zone? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. And on one occasion when I came to pick up some personal belongings in April, there was a lot of shooting from the woods. On that occasion I fell. I spent a month in the hospital after that. There was something wrong with my baby, and there was occasional shooting there all the time afterwards and I could hear it from where I was living in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And hadn't many Serb women and children left for Serbia for the very same reason?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All children and younger women had left the village. Only the elderly remained. On that particular day, I was the only one among younger women to be in Bjelovac together with her children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that since you weren't in Bjelovac for much of 1992 you don't know whether the VRS came to or through Bjelovac with tanks, artillery, or anything like that. That's not something you would know about. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be also right to say that you don't know -- or you didn't know much about the status of the TO or its relationship to the VRS or any of these military matters. That's not something which you knew about at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But you did tell us that - I hope I'm getting your evidence right - that everyone, I presume you meant every man, in Bjelovac was issued with a gun. Does that mean that hundreds of guns were distributed? Can you help us with that, with the number?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I cannot even tell you for sure how many people lived in Bjelovac because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This might be a convenient moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. How much more time do you have roughly do you guess, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm making a lot of progress. I imagine an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would appreciate, Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben, if we could finish by 12.30, in other words by the next break because something has come up that requires me to leave the building at 12.30 and then come back again for more work. In the meantime, I have got the new list -- amended witness list. Have you had it -- have you received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we just received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. For my part, I think I can undertake to be finished within an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's perfect. Let's continue. The accused is here, right. Everyone is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Filipovic, before the break I was asking you what you knew of military matters, and I think you were agreeing that you didn't know a great deal at the time. Had you heard bombs dropping before the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when you told us yesterday how you were inside a house and you were asked to estimate where the bombs were falling from the sound of their impact, that's the first time you had ever done that or the first time you'd experienced bombs falling in the vicinity, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you can't confidently assert, can you, that the bombs which you heard falling were not falling on the town of Bjelovac and were definitely falling on the woods or anything of that nature, can you?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a powerful explosion in the woods away from Bjelovac. Bombs were falling there. That's where you could hear explosions. They weren't falling in the area in which we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's pin that down. You heard some explosions in the woods. Can you say for sure that there weren't any explosions in the town of Bjelovac? Not just where you were but generally in the area of the village.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the part of the village in which we were staying, but further off, yes, you could hear explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Had you seen a Zolja being fired before the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you asked you before the break whether most of the people - by that I mean the attackers - were in civilian clothes. I want to just provide a reference for that now, and it's your 1994 statement, ERN 03090985. It's the fifth paragraph of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We don't need to turn to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But I suggest that you said: "Most of them, the attackers, were in," that's in square brackets, "were in civilian clothing." Now --

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both civilian clothing and camouflage uniforms. Now, as to whether more persons were wearing camouflage uniforms than civilian clothes, I really can't specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree that your recollection of these events might have been better in 1994 than they were -- than they are now?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your memory is better now than in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By that, I mean memory of what happened on the day. You're saying you have a clearer memory today, 2005, than you did in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that some of the people you saw wore ribbons. In a previous statement you said that they were wearing ribbons of all colours on their biceps. Do you agree that the ribbons were of all different colours?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically whether they were of all different colours, but they were predominantly red, worn around the biceps or as some sort of a headband. Mostly they were red, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So there were some which were of other colours?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I do remember that most were red.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, leaving aside able-bodied men, weren't there many Muslim women, children, and old men who came into your village on the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no children on that day, no young women. Mostly elderly persons and women, but they were in Bjelovac throughout, never leaving the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to clarify. I'm referring to Muslim women and children. Didn't they come into your village on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't they -- weren't the Muslim children present even when you were captured in your house who actually saw you being captured?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us --

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither women nor children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us how I think a few days later you saw people with bags coming from your village stuffed with goods. Didn't you also see that on the 14th of December, 1992, civilians with bags taking food?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the expression either at the time or later in Srebrenica "tobari" [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By that I'm referring to civilians who would go into villages with bags, Serb villages, to take food and possibly other items. Did you hear of that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But several days later, on our way to Srebrenica, in the village of Bjelovac itself, I came across a number of women, children, persons, that was on that specific day on our way through Bjelovac; they were carrying bags, sacks, bundles in their hands. That was all I could see on that day; that's not in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. You described how I think on the day of your capture and on subsequent days you saw Serb people who were dead in civilian clothes. And in answer to questions you stated that they didn't have rifles or other weapons on them. My question is: Are you aware from your time spent in Srebrenica that weapons were very scarce at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I can rephrase it. Were you aware that on the Muslim side there was such a shortage of weapons that front line soldiers wouldn't be given a weapon when they went to fight, that they would have to get it off a dead enemy, Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My suggestion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would -- I would have asked you how the Serb soldier would get killed in the first place if the Muslims are without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By another soldier and then -- Your Honour, there will be evidence, certainly, that one in four, or something of that nature, had a weapon and the others had to find weapons where they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So my suggestion, and I will put it as a suggestion, is that it would be very unusual in those times to see a corpse with a rifle or indeed with any weapon because very quickly someone would come along and take that weapon for themselves. Do you understand that suggestion and do you accept it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the bodies that I saw, I didn't pay any attention nor did it occur to me at any point in time to look whether there was a weapon lying nearby or not. It was quite enough for me to see the bodies. I would turn my head away that very instant. And on top of that, I did not really have time to study and inspect whether there was something lying next to those bodies. It only took a very short while for us to drive by.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was just that in answer to questions yesterday you did not assert repeatedly that you saw no weapons by those bodies, and that's why I ask. I want to refer to D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown a copy. I won't dwell for long on this subject, because it is no doubt a painful one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But you mentioned seeing the bodies of your brother-in-law and father-in-law, and I just ask you to look at this list. It's list of killed fighters, military post Bratunac. If you look at number 117, which in English is on page 5, we see the name Dragan Filipovic, and the birth date is 13/2/1962. Would you agree that's your brother-in-law, that refers to your brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You see two names down, Dragoljub Filipovic, born on the 25th of January, 1942. Do you agree that that's your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I'm not certain about the date of birth. But Filipovic, Dragoljub is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is your father -- your father-in-law's father, Milisav Djenalic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if we move further down, I think it's page 18 in the English, number 626, you see the name Milenko Mudzetic [phoen]. Is that the person you described as seeing on the 14th of December, 1992, outside your house and injured? Would he have been about 17 years old at the time? Number 626?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally at 229, which is page 8 in English, we see a name which in B/C/S it's Radenka Jovanovic, I think in the English it was mistranslated as Radenko. Daughter of Milosav. Does that refer to Duda who you referred to as a young girl that was pointed out to you by your mother-in-law but you didn't look at the corpse?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So was she actually 18 years old or more on the 14th of December, 1992, as opposed to being a young girl, as you described her?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was no longer a girl; she was a young woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for having to deal with these painful issues, and we'll move on. Now, going back to just when you were in your house, you described how men were shooting from the house while you were there with your children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness needs a break possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you all right to continue, Ms. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to have a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I think we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you need a break, we will give you a break. Could you pour her some water, please, usher. If you need to have a break, Madam, we'll have a short break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honours, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You described how men were shooting from your house. I just want to ask whether you would have felt safer at that moment out in the street with your children with you or whether you felt safer in the house at a moment?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at that time I think you described fierce fighting. Weren't Serbs also shooting back at the house where you were at that time? In other words -- I'll put the question again. When you were in your house, the Muslim fighters were at the window shooting at people, Serbs. They were being shot back at, weren't they, at that time, if you could judge it?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There was so much shooting all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see whether the Serbs who were shooting back were also shooting Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not able to see anything, being inside the house as I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that during that time even with all the shooting going on, the Muslims still took time to tend your wounds and your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. children's wounds?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. They didn't dress our wounds because they didn't have any bandages. But they allowed us to wipe the blood off because the wounds were bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned these people shooting Zoljas. Were the gases being discharged into this room while these weapons were being fired?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. The Zoljas were not being fired while we were still inside my house. They were firing those later when we were staying inside Stevo Filipovic's house. But I don't remember any gases coming in or being discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that because probably from what you saw you would be familiar with the fact that Zoljas discharge gases and that therefore a large number of them can't be fired in a confined space. I don't know if you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you seemed to be saying yesterday that if a Serb plane had been circling overhead in the morning of the 14th of December, 1992, and dropping bombs that you would have heard that despite the din of all the shooting. Is that correct? Was that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, nor did I ever say that. Even so, it's just not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that in fact a plane could have been circling in the morning and that you didn't hear it because of all the noise in the house?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would like to show you some segments of the video which were shown yesterday. It's Defence Exhibit D111.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so we need to switch, for the booth's benefit, to the Defence mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Filipovic, I'm just going to show you a bit of the video which you were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I propose to play from the beginning, to pause, and then we'll play a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Filipovic, I hope you can hear the voices while we play this video. For the record, I'm going to read the transcript into evidence. I can probably leave out the obscenity. "Did you see how the planes hit? Did you see how well they aim?" Now, I wonder whether you'd agree that when those people said that they weren't referring to how well the Serb planes aimed at the forest and how well they dropped their bombs in the woods -- MR. DI FAZIO: I object to that question, if Your Honours please. It's obviously asking this witness to tell you what's in the mind of the person who said those words. Who knows what that person is referring to. Who knows if he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are perfectly right, Mr. Di Fazio. Objection sustained. And Mr. Jones agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see the clock on the video says 9.35. Obviously I won't ask you to verify that time. But I'm going to ask you as we play the video to tell us whether you think it could be the morning and whether you hear the sound of cocks crowing, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we'll play four minutes of the video now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll pause it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, some questions, Ms. Filipovic. Do you agree that these pictures were taken from across the Drina looking over to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that these are Serbs discussing the attack, based on, one, where they're located, the Ekavian dialect, if you can hear that?

utterances.speaker: MIRA STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read the transcript, just the last bit into evidence. There's an older male voice saying: "Wait, the house was not on fire a short while ago." Younger mail voice: "A plane bombarded it. The plane just dropped a dozen of shells." Older voice: "And did it hit a truck as well?" Younger male voice: "Yes, it did. They are now on the houses." Perhaps it was not all interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it was not all interpreted in its entirety, then repeat it.
